title: Returning Memory, What Longing and Sleeplessness You Bring
intro: Abu Amr al-Shaybani connects the poem with an ambush laid by Bajila at a watering place. Asma’s barefoot apparition gives way to the poet running for his life, then climbing a bare peak in a patched sandal. When a critic challenges what he does with his money, he imagines going so far away that even those who know him cannot say where he is. Al-Mufaddal opened his anthology with this poem. Al-Nahari gives the love prelude three more verses than the anthology’s numbered text.

translation: Returning memory, what longing and sleeplessness you bring,
and a phantom crossing terrors to visit by night.
1.sharh: A recurring memory becomes someone he can address. While the lover lies awake, his mind supplies another figure on the move, a visitor willing to cross frightening country.

translation: It travels barefoot through weariness and snakes by night.
My life for you, traveller on your own two feet.
2.sharh: He offers his life for a visitor that can scarcely have feet to hurt. The hazards he gives the apparition anticipate a very physical account of what his own legs can do.

translation: The shade of a freeborn man’s daughter, once close to us.
After parting you went mad for her.
3.sharh: He identifies the visitor by her family and remembers an intimacy once taken for granted. Addressing himself at a distance, he finds desire all the fiercer since the separation.

translation: By God, can I trust a woman after Asma
swore such covenants and pledges by God?
4.sharh: Asma once put the strongest guarantee behind her word. He now invokes the same divine name to express what her conduct has done to his trust.

translation: She promises you everything you wish for and beguiles you,
like a flashing raincloud that passes over Dajnan.
5.sharh: The flash is real enough to raise hopes. The cloud moves on, leaving the watcher with the brightness of a promise and none of its water.

translation: When a loved one grudges her favours
and keeps hold with a few frail strands of affection,
6.sharh: She gives him just enough to keep him attached. Affection has dwindled to a few strands and the sentence itself hangs there until he tells us how he breaks away.

translation: I escape her as I escaped Bajila, when
at Khabt al-Raht by night I threw everything into my stride.
7.sharh: The verb for getting free carries him straight from love into danger. Having once had to outrun an enemy gives him a particularly vivid measure of getting clear of a lover.

translation: That night they shouted and set their fastest men on me
at the two thickets, where Ibn Barraq ran.
8.sharh: The shout starts the chase. Naming the thickets and his companion’s running ground gives the feat a location that another traveller might recognise.

translation: They might have been driving an ostrich with scant wing-feathers
or a fawn’s mother through shathth and tubbaq scrub.
9.sharh: From the pursuers’ side he might be an ostrich running on almost bare wings, or a doe in the scrub. Both animals make speed look like their native element.

translation: Nothing is faster than I, save the long-maned horse
and the wing beating beside the mountain ledge.
10.sharh: He measures himself against a horse by its mane and a bird by its wing. The usual reading makes them exceptions to his boast. Other commentators hear him claiming to beat even these.

translation: I got away before they could strip my gear,
running headlong, my strides short, my strength unspent.
11.sharh: Keeping his kit is proof of how completely he escaped. The words crowd together like his short, fast steps, with a suggestion of energy that still has plenty to spare.

translation: When a loved one breaks with me, I do not cry,
“Poor soul of mine, worn out with longing and fear.”
12.sharh: Coming back to the love story, he gives self-pity a perfectly recognisable voice. The next lines name the person for whom he would actually feel such grief.

translation: If ever I have cause to lament, my lament
is for a man quick to see how honour is earned,
13.sharh: He transfers the language of loss from the lover to a man fit to travel beside. Speed begins to mean seeing an honourable course of action before anyone else does.

translation: first to every finish-line of honour in his tribe,
his deep voice ringing out among the travelling bands.
14.sharh: The finishing posts are the distinctions a tribe can confer. Among men travelling together the companion has a deep carrying voice, as recognisable as his achievements.

translation: Lean-shinned, the sinews standing out along his arms,
he travels the dark night through sheets of pouring rain.
15.sharh: His bare shins and taut forearms show the work he is used to. Night and streaming rain then provide the conditions in which that body has to keep moving.

translation: A bearer of standards, ever present in council,
a speaker of sound words, a traveller to distant horizons.
16.sharh: Four phrases arrive in matched beats. They give the traveller a public voice as well as endurance, someone who can carry a standard, sit in council and say something worth hearing.

translation: That is the man I want, the man I turn to
when I need help, shaggy-haired, his voice a raven’s croak.
17.sharh: When he needs help, he turns to the companion he has just described. A shock of hair and a rough, carrying voice make the man as easily recognised at a distance as he is among the riders.

translation: His hair like a sand ridge worn crooked underfoot, I call him
master of two flocks, of lambs and halter loops.
18.sharh: The ridge is the shape of the man’s hair. Lyall hears a nickname for the comrade who looks after his fellows as a shepherd minds even the smallest lamb. Other readers hear a gibe at a herdsman.

translation: And many a peak that stands out like a spearhead,
open to the sun, scorching through the summer months,
19.sharh: The outline of the peak narrows to a point and offers no shade. He leaves us looking at the difficulty for a whole verse before the climbers appear.

translation: I raced my companions for its summit, no laggards they,
and climbed to it with the sun already up.
20.sharh: He is careful to give the others their due. Being first counts because these were strong climbers, and daylight has already exposed them to the heat.

translation: Nothing on its crag but the little wooden lookout,
part of it broken, part of it still standing.
21.sharh: He finds the remains of a lookout where a watcher once stood. A few broken sticks and a few upright ones are all the human company the summit affords.

translation: With a worn, ragged sandal to shield my toes,
I fitted a thong after laying sole on sole.
22.sharh: At the top he lets us see what he climbed in. A second layer of leather and a fastening he put in himself have been all that stood between the rock and his toes.

translation: Who will help me with this carping, faithless fault-finder
who has burnt my skin raw with blame?
23.sharh: The heat of the peak becomes the burning of words on skin. The string of names for the critic suggests the persistence of a voice that gives him no peace.

translation: He says, “You have squandered wealth that should have sufficed you,
good clothes, fine gear and things of price.”
24.sharh: We hear the critic directly. Clothes, equipment and valued possessions make an inventory, as if a lost life could be measured by counting up what is missing from the tent.

translation: My reprover, some blame is cruelty.
What possession lasts, however carefully you keep it?
25.sharh: The answer changes the measure of loss. Even what she persuaded him to save could never stay in his hands for ever.

translation: I give you my word, if you keep on blaming me,
the camp will ask about me at the ends of the earth.
26.sharh: He makes his departure conditional on what she does now. The scale of the threatened silence grows from one household to a whole encampment asking strangers for news.

translation: They will ask people who ought to know me,
yet no one they meet will bring them word of Thabit.
27.sharh: He gives the searchers the best possible witnesses and still withholds an answer. Using his personal name lets us hear how people might speak of him once he was gone.

translation: Meet your needs with the wealth you gather
until you meet what everyone must meet.
28.sharh: He pictures wealth used to plug the gaps in a life. The limit is the meeting everyone keeps, death, which he leaves unnamed.

translation: You will gnash your teeth in regret over me
one day, remembering something of the man I was.
29.sharh: The mouth that did the scolding will have another use, teeth striking together in regret. Even recalling a part of his character will be enough to make his absence felt.

1.1.2.head: عيد
1.1.2.meaning: Something that comes back upon a person, here a recurring memory.

1.2.5.head: طَرّاق
1.2.5.meaning: A habitual night visitor, here a phantom.

3.1.2-3.head: اِبنَةُ الحُرّ
3.1.2-3.meaning: “A freeborn man’s daughter”, the woman whose name follows in the next line.

3.2.2.head: اُجتُنَّ
3.2.2.meaning: Was driven out of his senses, here by love.

3.2.5.head: تِفِرّاق
3.2.5.meaning: Separation. Al-Ma'arri singles out the unusual form of this noun.

4.2.1.head: أَسماء
4.2.1.meaning: Asma, the woman whose apparition visits him.

5.1.3.head: أُمنِيَّة
5.1.3.meaning: Something wished for, here what the promise holds out.

5.1.4.head: غَرَّ
5.1.4.meaning: She holds out a false hope, like lightning that promises rain. The diwan and the studio text give taghurru, “deceives”. The consonant is hard to distinguish here from the one in tadurru, “does harm”.

5.2.4.head: ضَجنان
5.2.4.meaning: Dajnan, a mountain in the region of Mecca.

6.1.3.head: خُلَّة
6.1.3.meaning: A woman bound to him by affection.

6.1.5.head: نائِل
6.1.5.meaning: A favour bestowed, here affection given in return.

6.2.4.head: أَحذاق
6.2.4.meaning: Pieces or cut ends, here the frail remnants of a bond.

7.1.5.head: بَجيلَة
7.1.5.meaning: Bajila, the tribe from whose men he made his escape.

7.2.3-4.head: خَبتُ الرَّهط
7.2.3-4.meaning: Khabt al-Raht, a place named for an open stretch of low ground.

7.2.5.head: رَوق
7.2.5.meaning: “He cast forth his whole frame”, an expression for putting everything into a run.

8.2.1.head: العَيكَتان
8.2.1.meaning: Al-Aykatayn, “the two thickets”, a place in the account of the pursuit.

8.2.3-5.head: مَعدى اِبنِ بَرّاق
8.2.3-5.meaning: “Ibn Barraq’s running ground”, a place associated with his companion Amr ibn Barraq.

9.1.3-4.head: حُصّاً قَوادِمُه
9.1.3-4.meaning: “With close-cropped wing tips”, a male ostrich with little flight plumage.

9.2.3.head: خِشف
9.2.3.meaning: A young gazelle, here the calf of the running doe.

9.2.5-6.head: شَثّ وطُبّاق
9.2.5-6.meaning: Shathth and tubbaq, two shrubs associated with the Hijazi uplands.

10.1.6-7.head: ذو عُذَر
10.1.6-7.meaning: “The one with forelocks”, a horse known by its mane.

10.2.4.head: رَيد
10.2.4.meaning: A projecting rock or edge of a mountain.

11.1.5.head: سَلَب
11.1.5.meaning: The clothes and equipment a victor could strip from the defeated.

11.2.3-4.head: قَبيض الشَّدّ
11.2.3-4.meaning: “Short-drawn running”, rapid strides taken close together.

11.2.5.head: غَيداق
11.2.5.meaning: Abundant and freely flowing, transferred here to a runner’s energy.

13.1.2.head: عِوَل
13.1.2.meaning: Lamentation or crying out over a loss.

14.2.5.head: رِفقَة
14.2.5.meaning: A company travelling together, here several groups of companions.

15.1.2.head: ظُنبوب
15.1.2.meaning: The shinbone, prominent on his lean legs.

15.1.4.head: ناشِرَة
15.1.4.meaning: A sinew standing out along the forearm.

15.2.1.head: مِدلاج
15.2.1.meaning: One who travels far by night.

15.2.5.head: غَسّاق
15.2.5.meaning: Dark or pouring heavily, of a night black with rain.

16.1.4.head: نادٍ
16.1.4.meaning: A tribal meeting place where men confer.

17.1.3.head: غَزو
17.1.3.meaning: An aim or object of desire in this context.

17.2.3-4.head: ضافي الرَّأس
17.2.3-4.meaning: “Full about the head”, a man with a mass of hair.

18.1.2.head: حَدَّأَ
18.1.2.meaning: Bent something over into a hump.

18.2.2.head: ثَلَّة
18.2.2.meaning: A flock of sheep, here in the dual.

18.2.5.head: رِبق
18.2.5.meaning: A rope of loops used to tether lambs and kids.

19.1.1.head: قُلَّة
19.1.1.meaning: A mountain top, here an exposed summit.

20.1.2.head: قُنَّة
20.1.2.meaning: The very tip of the summit.

21.1.6.head: نَعامَة
21.1.6.meaning: A lookout erected on high ground.

21.2.2.head: هَزيم
21.2.2.meaning: Broken or fallen in, of the lookout.

22.2.3.head: سَريح
22.2.3.meaning: A leather thong used to fasten the sandal.

22.2.5.head: إِطراق
22.2.5.meaning: Layering leather to make or repair a sole.

23.1.4.head: خَذّالَة
23.1.4.meaning: Someone given to letting others down.

24.2.5.head: بَزّ
24.2.5.meaning: Personal gear, including fine clothing or arms.

26.2.6.head: أُفُق
26.2.6.meaning: A distant region or quarter of the world.

27.2.4.head: ثابِت
27.2.4.meaning: Thabit, the poet’s personal name, as it would be spoken by those searching for him.

28.1.2.head: خِلال
28.1.2.meaning: Gaps or wants to be made good.

29.1.1-3.head: قَرَعَ السِّنّ
29.1.1-3.meaning: “To strike the tooth”, to bite or grind one’s teeth in regret.
